A reader’s guide to restoration science and design

Source: RESEARCH-DESIGN-GUIDE.md

How can a restoration program make its collective knowledge easier to find, understand and use—across projects, disciplines and generations?

This guide is a starting point for program managers, scientists, restoration practitioners and partners who want to explore the work behind that question. It brings together selected research and development documents for the proposed science and restoration integration component of the the Upper Mississippi River Restoration (UMRR) Program’s Environmental Monitoring and Management Application (EMMA), supporting both UMRR and Navigation and Ecosystem Sustainability Program (NESP) communities.

The guide leads directly into the working documents in dev/. Those documents retain the evidence, design reasoning and unanswered questions behind the project. You can read the guide in order or start with a question that matters to you.

The report links below open draft HTML on the package website. When reading this Markdown file on GitHub, use the adjacent downloadable snapshot links and open the downloaded HTML in a browser. The reports are dated design prototypes; they are not approved assessments, live-system queries or comprehensive reviews.

Start here

If you have ten minutes, these three documents give a useful overview:

  1. Project purpose and direction — Why the initiative exists, the program context and the design directions established so far. Current project context.
  2. Bertom: three ways into the same evidence — A concrete example of starting from a research question, survey or project and following the connections among them. Bounded case review.
  3. Data model design report — The proposed information objects and relationships behind future reports, with examples and open decisions. Working conceptual design.

How to read the status labels

  • Source review: describes what was found in specified documents or data; its stated coverage and source limitations apply.
  • Case review: uses selected evidence to explore a real example; it is not necessarily a complete project history or scientific assessment.
  • Working design: a proposal for discussion and further validation, not an approved database schema or required workflow.
  • Prototype: an early implementation for testing ideas; its documented scope is narrower than the envisioned future system.
  • Accepted for further validation: a direction the project lead has accepted as a working pattern, with important details still open.
  • Deferred: material saved for a later conversation when the people or information needed are available.

The documents themselves are the source for their detailed status. In particular, a source-reported result, a proposed interpretation and an approved program decision are different things.

Some reports and design notes also refer to structured JSON worksheets and registers. The guide to structured research and design resources explains what each file contains, links to it and its companion review, and shows how to interpret record references such as SI-O3 and MS-03.

What is the initiative trying to accomplish?

The long-term vision is to help a practitioner begin with a question, study, project or other starting point and follow relevant connections toward both the ideas that motivated the work and the observations and judgments that followed. A useful report would explain why each connection appears and allow the reader to examine its supporting evidence.

  • Project purpose and direction — The initiative’s purpose, existing system anchors and current design boundaries. Current project context.
  • Model-guided evidence reports — How different starting points could lead readers through connected institutional knowledge and back to sources. Working design.
  • Strategic plan and FWWG review — How the work relates to the supplied draft 2025–2035 strategic plan and the Fish and Wildlife Working Group’s research-framework initiative. Source review; the plan remains draft.
  • Workshop research priorities — What the supplied workshop workbook records about research questions and reach-specific priorities, including limits on interpretation. Source review.

What might practitioners discover?

The cases use real program materials to test whether the emerging model can reveal useful relationships while retaining the limits of the evidence.

Bertom and McCartney Lakes: learning from an incomplete history

Historical project objectives, a rock habitat channel and a documented 2014 mussel survey provide a way to explore connections between restoration intent and monitoring. The user confirmed that EMMA has no recorded monitoring task for Bertom. The case illustrates why a missing task should not prevent people from using a historical report; it does not establish target attainment or project success.

  • View the Bertom multi-entry prototype — A curated evidence network with question, survey and project starting points; the optional future assessment is hypothetical. Draft snapshot, 2026-11-02. Downloadable snapshot.

  • View the Bertom evidence walkthrough — The earlier practitioner-oriented walkthrough of the same historical case. Draft snapshot, 2026-11-02. Downloadable snapshot.

  • Three starting points into one evidence network — Follow the same bounded case from a question, a survey or a project. Case review.

  • Bertom source and linkage review — The supporting documents, source locators, candidate connections and unresolved identity and spatial questions. Source review.

  • Bertom multi-entry report prototype — How the prototype presents selected views of a manually curated evidence network, including an optional, clearly hypothetical assessment. The page also gives instructions for generating the report locally. Prototype; not live-system discovery or a comprehensive search.

Steamboat Island: connecting science to a restoration opportunity

The Steamboat example explores the scientific basis and evaluation needs for an anticipated mussel-habitat benefit. It helps reveal the connections needed among restoration intent, research, possible study designs and evidence, without presenting an expected benefit as a demonstrated local effect.

  • View the Steamboat Island mussel report — A source-oriented case report connecting restoration intent, scientific evidence and evaluation questions, with links to its structured inputs. Draft snapshot, 2026-11-03. Downloadable snapshot.

  • Steamboat worked example — The case setup and available source materials. Case review.

  • Steamboat conceptual model — The concepts and relationships brought into focus by the case. Working design.

  • Research-question report notes — The Steamboat report and how the case-specific reporting work is produced and used in design. Prototype documentation.

Other comparisons

  • Cross-case linkage consolidation — What several cases reveal about representing connections across incomplete records. Case synthesis and working design.
  • Marsh Lake linkage review — A comparison from another restoration context, with limits on cross-program interpretation. Case review.

What information needs to be connected?

The proposed model brings together questions and hypotheses, study designs, restoration actions, observations, analyses, findings and subsequent judgments. It aims to make the meaning and basis of each connection visible, while referring back to authoritative systems and sources.

  • Data model design report — A consolidated view of the proposed objects, relationships, existing-system anchors and open choices. Working design.
  • Relational model and extraction roadmap — A first table-oriented logical sketch, enterprise and local prototyping boundaries, and retrieval-assisted document extraction. Working design; not production DDL.
  • Relational vertical slice — Reviewable ERDs, proposed fields and constraints, and Bertom/Steamboat examples for DuckDB development and later enterprise review. Working design.
  • DuckDB prototype and EMMA migration crosswalk — Run the local relational example and see how its tables correspond to existing EMMA structures. Local prototype; enterprise migration remains unverified.
  • Extraction quality and reprocessing plan — Future options for source provenance, human review, evaluation and incremental updates. Working design; detailed review and quality processes are deferred until after the MVP.
  • Science–restoration relationship analysis — The distinctions and relationships the cases suggest the model needs to preserve. Working design.
  • Minimum attributed linkage record — A proposed way to describe a relationship together with its source, scope, review state and responsibility. The project lead accepted this pattern for further validation; its fields and implementation remain open. Accepted for further validation.
  • EMMA crosswalk and Restoration Features review — How the design relates to the existing project information and GIS anchors. Source reviews and working crosswalks.

How can the program preserve learning and decisions?

Institutional learning depends on being able to recover not only data and reports, but also what practitioners concluded, how confident they were, what evidence they considered and how a decision evolved. The user has identified EMMA as the likely system of record for these practitioner-authored judgments for design purposes; the production schema, ownership and workflow remain to be determined.

  • Durable assessment and decision model — Proposed distinctions among findings, assessments, decisions and follow-up, and how they could remain tied to evidence. Working design.
  • HREP, performance-evaluation and workshop review — Program artifacts and context relevant to performance evaluation and learning across a project lifecycle. Source review.
  • FWWG learning-opportunity model — A proposed way to relate questions, potential opportunities, evidence and coordination. Working design, not an approved working-group process.

What have we learned from existing tools and models?

The project is looking for concrete ways to reuse existing work, especially open-source data models and tools that support science and adaptive-management information over time. A bounded review did not establish a complete open replacement for the envisioned UMRR function, but identified useful components and precedents.

  • Science and adaptive-management tooling watch — The candidate register, what was documented, what remains unverified and why each lead matters. Targeted review.
  • Bertom mapping to existing models — A limited comparison with AMMonitor, Miradi, SEPIO and AMModels, highlighting ideas for monitoring context, intended outcomes, evidence and analysis. Documentation-based comparison; not a tested import or approved schema.
  • Repeatable tooling-watch workflow — How the team can revisit promising implementations and licenses without repeatedly conducting a broad literature search. Proposed manual workflow.

What is still open?

The data model design report records the detailed questions. Among the decisions still to resolve are how records and identities will be managed across systems, how judgments will be reviewed and revised, and which evidence and relationships are needed for particular reports. Real cases also leave source, spatial and historical gaps that affect what can be concluded.

The team would like to hear directly from practitioners about the decisions and questions for which these reports would be useful. The FWWG practitioner discovery prompts preserve questions for that future conversation. Deferred; they are not statements of members’ preferences or evidence that interviews occurred.

How this guide relates to the agentic development framework

This repository also uses the reproducibleai-scaffolded agentic context to help people and coding agents maintain continuity. The guide gives human readers a curated view of that working material; it does not replace or modify the routing system.

  • AGENTS.md contains standing instructions and conditional routes: an agent starts with the documents relevant to its task instead of reading the entire project history.
  • Development context explains the dev/ structure and points to the maintained artifacts behind the work.
  • Artifact lifecycle describes how instructions, durable design material and checkpoints have distinct roles.
  • Current handoff is a concise resumption aid for a future development session; it is not a substitute for the underlying evidence and design documents.

The individual dev/ documents remain the maintained records for their topics. This guide is a curated orientation and should be updated when its links, descriptions or status labels no longer match them. The guide does not confer authority on a proposal or change the conditional routes in AGENTS.md.
